clinicalPearls: Secondary erythromelalgia is characterised by episodic burning pain, marked erythema and warmth of the extremities, most often the feet, triggered by heat, exercise or dependency and relieved by cooling and elevation.

Unlike the inherited primary form caused by SCN9A sodium-channel mutations, the secondary type arises from an identifiable underlying disorder, most classically a myeloproliferative neoplasm such as polycythaemia vera or essential thrombocythaemia.

Myeloproliferative-associated erythromelalgia frequently responds dramatically to low-dose aspirin, reflecting a platelet-mediated arteriolar inflammatory-thrombotic mechanism, a response that is a useful diagnostic clue.
Other secondary causes include connective-tissue disease, diabetes mellitus, peripheral neuropathy, drugs such as calcium-channel blockers and certain vasodilators, and paraneoplastic states.
Patients characteristically immerse affected limbs in cold water or seek cold surfaces for relief, which can lead to maceration, immersion injury or secondary infection.

A full blood count with examination of the film is mandatory in any adult presenting with erythromelalgia to exclude an occult myeloproliferative neoplasm, which may precede overt blood-count abnormalities.

Management targets the underlying cause together with symptom control using cooling, limb elevation, and agents such as aspirin for platelet-driven disease or neuropathic-pain modulators for neuropathic forms.
Aggressive cooling should be discouraged as prolonged immersion can precipitate ulceration, necrosis and infection, worsening long-term outcome.
reference.pathophysiology: Secondary erythromelalgia results from a maldistribution of skin blood flow in which there is inappropriate arteriovenous shunting and microvascular hypoperfusion despite overall increased flow and erythema, so tissue oxygenation is paradoxically reduced during attacks. In myeloproliferative disease, abnormal, hyperreactive platelets adhere to and inflame arteriolar walls, producing platelet-fibrin thrombi and a local inflammatory response that generates burning pain and compensatory vasodilatation; this platelet-driven mechanism underlies the striking sensitivity to aspirin. In neuropathic and connective-tissue-associated forms, dysregulation of small-fibre sensory and autonomic nerves alters vasomotor control and nociceptive signalling. Heat and dependency lower the threshold for symptomatic vasodilatation, while cooling and elevation reduce metabolic demand and shunting, temporarily relieving symptoms.
additionalDifferentials: Peripheral arterial disease with rest pain
additionalInvestigations: Full blood count and peripheral blood film to detect myeloproliferative neoplasm
JAK2 V617F and related myeloproliferative mutation testing
Fasting glucose and HbA1c to assess for diabetes mellitus
Autoimmune serology including antinuclear antibodies for connective-tissue disease
Nerve conduction studies and small-fibre assessment (e.g. skin biopsy for intraepidermal nerve fibre density)
Medication review to identify vasodilator or other drug triggers
Screening for occult malignancy where a paraneoplastic cause is suspected
redFlags: Abnormal full blood count or splenomegaly suggesting an underlying myeloproliferative neoplasm
Digital ulceration, necrosis or gangrene from disease or excessive cooling
Signs of secondary infection following repeated cold immersion
Rapidly progressive neurological deficit accompanying the limb symptoms
Systemic features suggesting occult malignancy or active connective-tissue disease
reference.prognosis: Prognosis largely follows the underlying cause; platelet-driven myeloproliferative erythromelalgia often improves markedly with treatment of the neoplasm and aspirin, whereas neuropathic and idiopathic secondary forms tend to be chronic and harder to control.
pitfalls: Failing to check a full blood count and thereby missing an occult myeloproliferative neoplasm
Mistaking the warm, red painful limb for cellulitis and prescribing unnecessary antibiotics
Permitting prolonged cold immersion, which causes maceration, ulceration and infection
Assuming all erythromelalgia is primary and overlooking a treatable secondary trigger such as a drug
Attributing symptoms to peripheral arterial disease and missing the diagnosis
management: Identify and treat the underlying cause, such as a myeloproliferative neoplasm, connective-tissue disease, diabetes mellitus or peripheral neuropathy
Low-dose aspirin, which is dramatically effective in myeloproliferative-associated disease
Withdraw provoking drugs including calcium-channel blockers and other vasodilators
Symptomatic cooling and elevation, counselling against cold-water immersion that causes maceration, immersion injury and infection
Refer to haematology where a myeloproliferative neoplasm is suspected, repeating blood counts as it may precede overt count abnormalities
Skin and wound care with treatment of secondary infection
